body.heading: Fire under the sea
paragraphs: Most of Earth’s volcanoes are hidden. They erupt on the sea floor, where lava cools in dark pillows and piles up, layer on layer, over thousands of years.
Sometimes the pile wins. When an undersea volcano grows tall enough to break the surface, a new island stands where charts used to show only water.

body.heading: Islands people watched being born
paragraphs: The Hawaiian Islands formed this way, one after another, as the Pacific Plate drifted slowly over a hot spot in Earth’s mantle. The youngest island is still growing at its south-eastern edge today.

In 1963, off the coast of Iceland, the sea itself began to boil and steam, and within days a brand-new island — Surtsey — stood above the waves. Scientists have watched it ever since: first bare rock, then seeds arriving on the wind, then plants, birds and seals colonising land younger than the researchers studying it.

body.heading: Builders and destroyers
paragraphs: Volcanoes have a fearsome reputation, and they have earned it. But the same forces also build: new land, rich volcanic soils that farmers prize, and whole ecosystems from scratch.
An island is a reminder that Earth’s surface is not finished. It is still under construction.

takeaway: Islands like Hawaii and Surtsey began as underwater eruptions — volcanoes are Earth’s land-building machines.
